notes: Groceries are taxed at 5% since July 1, 2025 (7% before). Of the two cities with a general tax, Tupelo's 0.25% has applied to groceries since May 1, 2026 and Jackson's 1% doesn't apply to them.

Alcohol is taxed at 7% at retail (since July 1, 2022 for liquor and wine), on top of excise taxes (wine 35 cents a gallon, sparkling wine $1.00, spirits $2.50; Miss. Code 27-72-7) and the state's markup on liquor and wine, left out here.
Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at 7%, on top of excise taxes left out here: 68 cents a pack of cigarettes and 15% of the list price on other tobacco.
Household supplies: diapers are taxed in full; a 2026 bill to exempt them (HB 491) wasn't taken up.
Personal care products: menstrual products are taxed in full; they aren't on the Department of Revenue's list of exemptions.
Barber and beauty services: not taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).
Clothing is taxed, except clothing, footwear and school supplies under $100 during the holiday of July 10 to 12, 2026 (cities may opt out).
Laundry and dry cleaning: laundering and dry cleaning are taxed.
Motor fuel is exempt from the sales tax and taxed by the gallon instead: 24 cents for gasoline from July 1, 2026 (27 cents from July 1, 2027) plus a 0.4-cent environmental fee, left out here.
Auto repair labor: vehicle repair is taxed.

Local tourism taxes on restaurants (usually 1% to 3%) are counted in the restaurant rate where the Department of Revenue lists them, a county's on top of its cities'; some also fall on alcohol bought in stores: Hattiesburg's 2% on package liquor stores and Oxford's 2% on beer and liquor sold outside them, counted there on liquor stores' share of alcohol bought in stores (and the rest), from the 2022 Economic Census (the cities' notes give it); Laurel's on certain sales of alcoholic beverages isn't counted.
Hotel stays pay the 7% sales tax plus local hotel taxes where levied (1% to 5%, and in some places a nightly fee: Gulf Coast hotels in Harrison County pay 12% in all), which aren't counted here.
The services below are from the Department of Revenue's sales tax rates page.
gaps: Mississippi counties have no general sales tax. Two cities have general ones: Jackson (1%, not on groceries, hotel rooms or larger restaurants) and Tupelo (0.25%, groceries included since May 1, 2026).

Local tourism taxes on restaurant sales (usually 1% to 3%) are counted in the restaurant rate, read from the Department of Revenue's description of each levy; a county's levy is added to its cities' own. Hotel-only levies are not counted.
Groceries are taxed at 5% instead of 7% (state), counted in the grocery category rather than the general rate.

Restaurant levies set to end in 2027 unless the Legislature extends them (counted here; each noted on its page): Baldwyn Tourism Tax (July 1, 2027); Batesville Tourism and Economic Development Tax (July 1, 2027); Carrollton Tourism, Parks and Recreation Tax (July 1, 2027); Charleston Tourism, Parks and Recreation Tax (July 1, 2027); Lexington Tourism, Parks and Recreation tax (July 1, 2027); Lucedale Restaurant Tax (July 1, 2027); North Carrollton Recreation, Tourism, Parks and Economic Development Tax (July 1, 2027); Pearl Tourism, Recreation and Parks Tax (July 1, 2027); Waynesboro Tourism Parks and Recreation Tax (July 1, 2027); Eupora Tourism Tax (September 30, 2027); Grenada Tourism Tax (September 30, 2027); Grenada Tourist and Convention Tax (September 30, 2027).

Levies whose repeal date has passed are left out: Columbus Tourism Promotion and MUW Support Tax (ended July 1, 2018); Como Tourism Tax (ended July 1, 2013); Sardis Tourism Tax (ended July 1, 2026); Vaiden Tourism, Parks and Recreation Tax (ended July 1, 2022).
Restaurant levies on part of a city only are not recorded: Pearl (West) Restaurant Tax.

tiers.label: Mississippi county tier (jobs tax credit)
tiers.what: Determines the county's designation for Mississippi's jobs tax credit and other tier-based incentives; Tier 3 (less developed) counties get the largest per-job credit and Tier 1 (developed) the smallest. The ranking sheet itself does not list credit amounts.

programs: No tax increment financing districts or business improvement districts are mapped: Jackson, Hattiesburg (the District at Midtown) and Gulfport publish no district maps, and Downtown Jackson Partners' district has none. No current list of the state's Growth and Prosperity counties was found: the Mississippi Development Authority certifies them county by county on unemployment and poverty rates set in the program's rule (6 Miss. Code R. 1-12.2), and publishes no list. Main Street districts aren't mapped: Mississippi Main Street lists 49 designated communities (msmainstreet.com, October 30, 2026): Aberdeen, Amory, Baldwyn, Batesville, Biloxi, Booneville, Brandon, Byhalia, Cleveland, Clinton, Columbia, Columbus, Corinth, Crystal Springs, Greenville, Greenwood, Gulfport, Hattiesburg, Hernando, Indianola, Itawamba County, Laurel, Leake County (Carthage), Louisville and Noxapater, Magee, Meridian, Moss Point, Natchez, Nettleton, New Albany, Ocean Springs, Okolona, Pascagoula, Pass Christian, Pearl, Philadelphia, Picayune, Pontotoc County, Ripley, Saltillo, Senatobia, Starkville, Sumrall, Tunica, Tupelo, Vicksburg, Water Valley, West Point and Woodville (Brandon and Magee new in 2026), plus three network communities (Jackson's Farish Street Historic District, Long Beach and Olive Branch).

warn.text: Mount Pleasant's visitor caution draws on its census tract's homes the Census counts as seasonal (237 of 1,785, 13.3%, with 1 lodging place), which may be weekend or hunting places rather than a tourist trade, so read that caution with care.

Gulfport draws many visitors (its beaches and the Mississippi Aquarium), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Ocean Springs draws many visitors (its downtown, beaches and arts), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Philadelphia draws many visitors (the nearby Pearl River Resort's casinos), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Pearl River draws many visitors (the Pearl River Resort's casinos), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Tunica draws many visitors (the Tunica casinos and the Delta's blues sites), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: {visitor_why} (its page is built from the census tract it shares with North Tunica and Austin). Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Clarksdale draws many visitors (its blues heritage and festivals), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Greenville draws many visitors (its casinos), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: {visitor_why}. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
Fayette's visitor caution draws on its census tract's seasonal homes (84 of 464, 18.1%) with no lodging places, likely hunting land more than a tourist trade, so read that caution with care.
Osyka's visitor caution draws on its census tract's seasonal homes (279 of 2,156, 12.9%) with no lodging places, likely hunting land more than a tourist trade, so read that caution with care.

Dublin's flag as a visitor economy draws on the motels in the census tract it shares with Clarksdale and Lyon (8 lodging places, 2.9 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers on the highways into Clarksdale, so read that flag with care.

Escatawpa's flag as a visitor economy draws on its hotels and motels along Interstate 10 (13 lodging places, 2.9 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.

Helena may carry the visitor caution only because of the hotels and motels along Interstate 10 in its census tract (5 lodging places, 3.3 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that caution with care.

Toomsuba may carry the visitor caution only because of the hotels and motels along Interstate 20 east of Meridian in the census tract it shares with Marion (16 lodging places, 5.4 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that caution with care.

Mississippi State's flag as a visitor economy draws on the hotels near the university in its census tract (14 lodging places, 2.7 per 1,000 residents), which serve visitors to the university, so read that flag with care.
